name: East Ridge (Inspiration Glacier)

ways.name: Eldorado Creek climbers' path to Inspiration Glacier high camp
ways.season: Jul-Sep, once the talus is bare
ways.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount roughly 20 miles to the Eldorado parking area at about 2,100 ft. The first ten miles are paved; the rest is gravel and washboard.

The path does not leave from the parking area. Walk back down the road about 90 feet and look for the log (historically a large single log, sometimes a clump of trees) spanning the Cascade River. The crossing shifts year to year and is slick when wet — a handline is worth carrying for a party that is not confident on a log. On the far bank walk perpendicular to the river roughly 100 feet to pick up the boot path.

The path climbs steeply and relentlessly through old-growth timber with no water, gaining about 1,500 ft before it breaks out into the boulder field. Follow cairns and flagging up the boulders, staying climber's right so you do not cross Eldorado Creek unnecessarily. The boulder field is universally described as the worst part of the trip, and worse on the way down with a heavy pack.

Above the boulders the ground eases into Eldorado Creek Basin (roughly 5,400-5,600 ft, about 3 miles and 3,300 ft from the car), a common first camp. To continue, climb onto the rocky ridge at about 6,100 ft and drop a few hundred feet on the far side into Roush Creek Basin (6,100-6,400 ft, running water). From Roush, broken talus and slabs lead onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier; rope up here. Moderate glacier slopes lead to high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration saddle around 7,500-7,800 ft.

Overnight stays need a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. Eldorado is a high-use cross-country zone; there is an advance lottery and reservations on Recreation.gov, but permits for the areas off Cascade River Road (Eldorado, Boston Basin, Cascade Pass) must be picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

ways.name: Late-spring snow cover (skis or boots)
ways.season: late May-June
ways.notes:
In late spring the upper approach is continuous snow and the boulder field problem largely disappears, which is why many parties prefer this window. It does not make the whole approach snow: a late-May park report described the route as snow-free until just before Eldorado Basin was gained around 5,000 ft, with the boulder fields completely melted out — so expect a dry, steep forest climb first and snow only above.

Ski parties commonly carry ski boots and walk the forest section in approach or running shoes, switching over at snow line.

The trade is avalanche exposure. Large avalanches sweep parts of this route in winter and spring, and Cascade River Road itself can be buried by avalanche debris miles below the trailhead in a heavy year, adding road miles before you even start.

priorPrimaryResearch: Eldorado Creek climbers' path in summer is the standard; variant 1 is the same line under late-spring snow.

ways.name: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the meadow camp
ways.season: Mid-July into early October. Snow can hold in the gullies well into the season, and an axe is worth carrying early and mid-season.
ways.notes: Drive the Entiat River Road and then the switchbacking forest-road spur to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, and follow North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 up-valley. Almost all of the distance to the peak is on trail. The usual staging point is the trail camp in the meadow below the summit around 6,700 ft, and the climb starts from the tread a short way north of it. A boat-access alternative exists on the far side, reaching the peak from Emerald Park via Trail #1230 out of the lakeshore settlement; it is a genuine second way in, but where that line joins the climbing is unclear, so the base-finding below is written for the trail camp side.

ways.name: Emerald Park trail from Lucerne
ways.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, follow the Domke Lake trail to the Emerald Park trail, and climb up Emerald Park to Milham Pass, which drops into the basin between Emerald and Saska. A boat-dependent alternative to the Entiat side, and the natural choice when coming from Lake Chelan.

ways.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, to the left side of the south face
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
The shared Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boulder field at the south end, and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft of loose scree in 1.25 miles, hazardous under snow into early July.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way from the trailhead.

Five pitches, about 450 ft: a burly and somewhat dirty roof pitch straight off the deck, an exposed corner to a good ledge, a short aid section through steep ground, a fingery crack between two features, and then the final corner crack shared with the neighbouring line to finish.

Because it joins that neighbour near the top, it shares its descent: a single full-length rappel on the north side and about thirty minutes of scrambling back round to the base.

ways.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
ways.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to Prusik Pass and round onto the west face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.

ways.name: Basalt Ridge crest to Fifth of July Pass
ways.season: Mid-July through early October, and popular in early autumn for the larch.
ways.notes: This is the shorter alternative to the Entiat River approach. From the Basalt Pass trailhead, climb to the pass — the small stream in the gully below it is the last water, and there is none at all beyond — then follow the ridge north. The trail bypasses the first high point about 300 ft below it, and beyond the trail fork the tread fades into slick pumice. Continue north past the neighbouring tower's saddle, then through a col around 7,480 ft on the next peak's southwest ridge, dropping through a scree gully into the basin west of it. Hop the massive boulders in that basin, cross a small larch meadow, and regain the ridge. The peak can also be reached from the Entiat River side by way of Myrtle Lake, the Larch Lakes and Cow Creek Pass — that is the line the main approach and waypoints describe; the marks below are written for this Basalt Ridge side.

ways.name: Entiat River and Larch Lakes
ways.notes: From the trailhead at the end of the Entiat River road, follow the Entiat River trail up the valley and climb the side trail to the Larch Lakes meadows. From a camp between the lakes the summit is a modest day out along the ridge. Longer than the Basalt Ridge line, but on maintained trail with water, so it suits multi-day trips and loops.

ways.name: Devore Creek Trail from Bird Creek Camp over the Enigma saddle
ways.season: Midsummer into early autumn, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends.
ways.notes: Come up the lake by passenger ferry or floatplane, ride the shuttle up the valley road to the bridge, cross it and follow the road past the camp and the airstrip to pick up the river trail. Follow that mostly flat trail southeast to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction, then climb steeply through rock bluffs and open forest into the wilderness and traverse brushy, dry hillside to Bird Creek Camp — the only designated camp in that stretch of trail, sitting about fifty yards before the creek crossing, with room for about three tents and a cook area. From camp the peak is a long day of its own; it does not combine with the neighbouring summit above the same camp, and every account allows a full day for each.

ways.name: Holden Village over Tenmile Pass
ways.notes: From Holden, climb to Tenmile Pass, descend the shoulder into upper Riddle Creek, then traverse northeast into the Castle Creek basin to join the standard line around 6,500 ft. Longer and more involved than Devore Creek; mostly used to combine Flora with Riddle Peak, or by parties exiting to Holden after climbing from Stehekin.

name: West Ridge

ways.name: South face couloir to the West Ridge notch
ways.season: Jun–early Aug, while it still holds snow
ways.notes: From the Boston Basin high camp, traverse up and east across talus and the remains of the Quien Sabe Glacier toward Forbidden's south face. Where the glacier is melted out, a class 3 rock spur on climber's right is usually faster and drier than staying on snow; where it is snow-covered or crevassed, rope up. The couloir itself runs about 500 ft and steepens to 40–50° near the top, which is where crampons and an axe stop being optional. Reaching the notch is roughly 2,000 ft above camp.

ways.name: Cat Scratch gullies (late season, once the couloir has melted out)
ways.season: Late Aug–Sep, dry conditions
ways.notes: When the couloir has gone to loose talus and scree, the usual line moves off the snow onto the rock gully system immediately west — climber's left — of it. Roughly the first 200 ft is class 4, easing to grassy class 3 for the last 200 ft to the notch. It is loose the whole way, and it is slower than it looks on the approach.

priorPrimaryResearch: The south-face couloir is the standard line to the West Ridge notch for most of the season. The Cat Scratch gullies are the late-season fallback once it melts out. The paragraph describes Boston Basin and the couloir. The seasons already differ.

name: Frostbite Ridge

ways.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the 7,200 ft camp
ways.season: Jun-Sep
ways.notes:
The White Chuck River Trail was destroyed by a 2003 flood and has no road or trail access, so this approach is no longer usable; reach Kennedy Ridge from White Pass on the PCT instead. The old line ran from the White Chuck River trailhead at about 2,300 ft. Follow the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) about six miles to the Kennedy Ridge Trail (FST 639) junction, then Kennedy Ridge Trail about a mile and three quarters to the PCT.

Head north on the PCT past the Glacier Creek crossing, which is your water, to an unmarked climbers' path leaving the trail on Glacier Ridge about two thirds of a mile beyond the creek. That path climbs snow and pumice to the standard high camp near 7,200 ft on the Kennedy Ridge shoulder.

ways.name: Suiattle River Road and the PCT via Milk Creek
ways.season: Jun-Sep
ways.notes:
Drive the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) from Darrington to its end at Sulphur Creek Campground. Follow the Suiattle River trail about seven miles to the bridge over the river, then the PCT southbound about nine miles to a camp in the East Fork Milk Creek basin at about 5,600 ft. From there continue up the ridge on snow and pumice to the same standard high camp near 7,200 ft.

The Suiattle River Road has a long history of flood damage and multi-year closures, so its status is worth confirming rather than assuming.

ways.name: North Fork Sauk to White Pass, then north
ways.season: Jun-Sep
ways.notes: Some parties use the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass — about nine miles and 5,900 ft — and then make a long traverse north on or near the PCT to the same Kennedy Ridge camp area. It is a twenty-mile-plus approach day and is chosen when the other two roads are out.

priorPrimaryResearch: USFS lists White Chuck River Trail 643 and Kennedy Ridge Trail 639 as INACCESSIBLE (washed out 2003, no plans to repair), so variant 0 is obsolete. Recent Frostbite trip reports (Hebert 2022, Mountaineers 2023/2025, WTA) all start at North Fork Sauk and go north on the PCT over Red Pass. Prose mainly describes the dead White Chuck/Kennedy Ridge line (variant 0), with N Fork Sauk as option 2.

ways.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the Glacier Creek camps
ways.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, and it is one of the shorter windows on the mountain — the upper Kennedy is a small, steep glacier that opens into a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses as the season runs on
ways.notes:
The historic line starts at the White Chuck River Trailhead at the end of FR-23 and follows Trail #643 about four miles, then Kennedy Ridge Trail #639 for 1.7 miles to the Pacific Crest Trail near 5,000 ft. Turn north on the PCT and follow it about two miles to the Glacier Creek crossing, where there are established camps with reliable water near 5,300 ft. Four to five hours is the usual pack-in.

FR-23 has been closed from milepost 3.7 to its end, so the reliably open option in recent seasons has been the North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass to the same Glacier Creek camps. That is a much longer walk to the same place, and it changes nothing above camp.

From the Glacier Creek camp a climbers' trail runs up a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge. Everything above is glacier, and the character of the day is set by how well you read the upper glacier rather than by any technical difficulty — the headwall at the top is about 40 degrees and short, while the crevasse field below it is the part parties spend hours on.

ways.name: North Fork Sauk and the crest trail north
ways.notes: Walk the North Fork Sauk trail up the valley and climb to the crest trail near White Pass, then follow it north past Red Pass, across the White Chuck basin and on toward Kennedy Creek, descending to the bench below the glacier. Long, with real elevation loss on the way, but this is how most parties now reach the Kennedy side.

name: Sitkum Glacier

ways.name: North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass
ways.season: Jun-Aug
ways.notes: The way in since the White Chuck side closed. North Fork Sauk Trail #649 runs up the valley through old growth to Mackinaw Shelter and then switchbacks steeply to the Pacific Crest Trail at about 5,950 ft, roughly eight to nine miles from the trailhead. Turn north on the PCT, cross Red Pass a mile or two on, and descend into the upper White Chuck valley, following the PCT down it for roughly seven to nine miles past the old White Chuck River Trail junction to Sitkum Creek. It is much longer than the old approach, and the climb back over Red Pass comes on the way out.

ways.name: White Chuck River Trail #643 (closed since the 2003 flood)
ways.season: Jun-Aug
ways.notes:
This was the standard way up Glacier Peak until the October 2003 flood. The White Chuck Road (FR 23) is now closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7 and the trail has been listed as inaccessible since the flood, so this is kept as a record of the old line rather than as a way in.

From the trailhead at about 2,350 ft the trail runs upstream through old growth, crossing Pumice, Glacier and Kennedy Creeks — reliable water, but high with snowmelt in early summer. At about five and a half miles is the old Kennedy Hot Springs area at around 3,300 ft, still a popular campsite; the pool, lodge and guard station were destroyed by the 2003 flood and never rebuilt, so there is no usable hot pool there.

Another mile and a half brings you to Sitkum Creek and the PCT junction at about 3,850 ft. Turn north on the PCT for about half a mile to a forested camp near 4,100 ft.

priorPrimaryResearch: White Chuck trail is the historic, route-defining approach to the Sitkum and the road was reopened (WTA signpost; a Feb 2025 NWHikers report reached the road end); North Fork Sauk is the longer fallback. Dec 2025 storm damage limits Glacier Peak Wilderness access now, so recheck.

name: Golden Age

ways.name: Up the gully to its own ledge
ways.notes: From the pullout near milepost 166, hike the gully below the wall for about an hour and follow a narrow ledge back right to the start, a prominent left-arching wide corner. The direct way, and the most practical when the gully is in shape.

ways.name: Via the centre route's lower pitches
ways.season: Summer, once the wall has dried; the pitches used to reach it are the same ones that seep into early summer in wet years.
ways.notes: You can scramble on up the gully to this climb's own ledge, but many parties add pitches instead: do the usual gully approach from the pullout near milepost 166 to the wall's upper ledge, then climb the lower pitches of the centre eleven-pitch line to the shared midway ledge system and traverse left from there. Rack for the pitches you are climbing to get there as well as for this route.

ways.name: Via the right-hand cave route's lower pitches
ways.season: Summer, once the wall has dried.
ways.notes: The same idea from the other side: climb the lower pitches of the right-hand cave line off the upper ledge to reach the shared midway ledge system, then traverse left. This is the longer leftward traverse of the two, so allow for it.

priorPrimaryResearch: Variant 1 calls itself the longer leftward traverse and mainly the descent line, which makes the centre-route start the usual way up. The paragraph names both starting routes equally.

name: Southeast Slopes (Standard Scramble)

ways.name: Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 over Baldy and along the crest
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. North-facing gullies on the last stretch hold steep snow into July
ways.notes:
There is no roadside access to this ridge; the drive only gets you to the trailhead at the end of FR-2860-120, off FR-2870 / Lost Mountain Road, itself off Palo Alto Road south of US-101 near Sequim. Road-end parking at a dirt berm, about 3,300 ft, Northwest Forest Pass required.

Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 leaves the berm on an old roadbed and crosses Mueller Creek almost immediately — the last easy reliable water for a long stretch, so fill up. The trail narrows to single-track around 0.3 mile and then turns relentlessly steep, gaining roughly 3,000 ft in a little over two miles of fall-line tread with essentially no switchbacks, in places barely a boot-width across eroded crumbly ravine crossings and slopes of packed dirt and shattered shale. It is a climber's path, not a graded trail.

At about 2.7 miles and 6,200 ft it tops out on the saddle between Tyler Peak and Baldy, where a short steep side path drops off the crest to a snowmelt spring — the last dependable water on the route.

ways.name: Royal Basin and the east face, for a traverse rather than an out-and-back
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
The other end of the same ridge, and the reason to know it is that it turns this route into a traverse instead of a there-and-back over Baldy twice. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, the Royal Basin Trail leads to Royal Lake and Upper Royal Basin. From the ridge, the east face drops roughly 3,000 ft to intersect the Royal Basin Trail.

It is steep, loose and only lightly travelled: packed dirt and shattered shale, brushy notches, and picking through timber looking for blazes and cairns. Some parties scree-ski the looser upper sections rather than rope up at all. It is not a bolted or standardised line — where parties do rope down a short cliffy step, anchors are improvised from trees or natural rock horns.

Most commonly this is used as the exit after climbing from Maynard Burn, closing a loop out Royal Basin or back over the ridge.

priorPrimaryResearch: Lower Maynard Burn/Baldy is the SE Slopes approach; Royal Basin variant is only for making a traverse.

name: Southeast Route

ways.name: Barclay Creek climbers' path — summer line
ways.season: June to September. Early June parties meet significant lingering snow and heavy brush; late July through August is typically the clearest.
ways.notes: From the Barclay Lake trailhead, do not take the maintained lake trail. Walk back down the access road about a quarter mile and pick up the old deactivated spur road — parties who know it often park at the spur's gated start instead of the main lot. Follow the old roadbed a hundred or two hundred yards to a fire-pit clearing, turn right, and pick up the unmarked but well-trodden climbers' path. It drops to the creek and crosses on a log jam or by rock-hopping near the downstream tip of a small mid-channel island; this crossing is the main early-season hazard. On the far bank the path swings west, then north, and starts climbing in earnest through sustained tight switchbacks in second-growth timber. Two decision points follow. Around thirty-six to thirty-eight hundred feet the path forks near a band of exposed rock — stay right and do not scramble the outcrop straight ahead, which is a known trap; the correct line keeps traversing climber's-left beneath a cliff band. Then around forty-four hundred feet the summer line bends left up a brushy weakness in the cliff band rather than continuing up the couloir, which holds snow late. Huckleberry and heather meadows lead to the saddle at about fifty-four hundred feet, the last reliable water.

ways.name: Tailgunner couloir — snow-season line
ways.season: Late spring, while the couloir holds continuous consolidated snow. Once it starts melting out it becomes the wrong answer and the summer line through the brushy weakness is correct.
ways.notes: The same start — the spur road, the fire-pit clearing, the creek crossing at the island, and the switchbacks up through the timber. The difference comes at about forty-four hundred feet: instead of bending left into the brushy weakness in the cliff band, the snow-season line continues directly up the couloir to the saddle. This same couloir is a documented wrong turn in summer and an avalanche path, so it is only reasonable when it is a continuous snow climb and conditions have been assessed.

priorPrimaryResearch: The Barclay Creek climbers' path is the summer standard, and Tailgunner is a snow-season variation. The paragraph describes variant 0.
